title: Estimating sparse finite-field matrix rank with sublinear queries
formal: For each fixed integer \(d\ge1\) and fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), determine up to constant factors the randomized adaptive row/column-query complexity \(Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\) of estimating \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}(A)\) within additive \(\varepsilon n\), for all \(n\times n\) binary matrices with at most d ones in every row and column, with success probability at least \(2/3\).
definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses arithmetic modulo two. Rank is the dimension of the span of the columns over that field, and belongs to \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\). Both row and column degree bounds are promises; there are no symmetry or graph-incidence promises. The all-zero matrix and zero rows or columns are allowed.

A row query gives a label \(i\in[n]\) and receives the complete list of indices j for which \(A_{ij}=1\), in increasing order. A column query analogously returns every i with \(A_{ij}=1\). Each list query costs one, and contains at most d indices. Query choices may depend on all previous answers and random coins. There is no free access to matrix-vector products or uniformly random nonzero entries. Random row or column labels can be chosen internally, but their lists still cost queries.

Define \(Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\) as the minimum worst-case number of queries of a randomized decision tree returning a real estimate r with \(\Pr[|r-\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}(A)|\le\varepsilon n]\ge2/3\) on each eligible matrix. Arbitrary computation on the transcript is free. Query complexity is at most n by reading every row. The asymptotic limit is n tending to infinity with d and accuracy fixed; matching constants may depend on both. This is not an algorithm whose total time must be sublinear.

The original problem list includes rectangular matrices over finite fields; the imported card selected square matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\). For binary matrices, the neighbor lists determine all nonzero values, so the interface is complete. Its conjectured general linear lower bound should mean a fixed nontrivial degree and accuracy regime, not a claim for every d: the d=1 class, for example, has much simpler rank structure.
answer_criterion: Provide complete Lean-checked matching upper and lower asymptotic query bounds in the stated interface for the fixed-parameter regimes, identifying any regime changes. A lower bound for solving Ax=b with an independently hidden right-hand side does not establish a lower bound for estimating rank of A alone. A theorem for real-valued rank or unbounded sparsity concerns a different problem. The precision sought is asymptotic constant-factor query complexity, not absolute 1/100 evaluation of the query-count function.
context:
Yoshida’s 2014 problem list asks for bounded-degree finite-field rank estimation and conjectures a linear-query obstruction in general. It also explains why rank is easier in a binary graph-incidence special case.

The question is information-theoretic: the challenge is what row and column neighborhoods reveal, independent of the cost of linear algebra on a fully learned matrix. The square binary specialization was already selected at import and is retained explicitly.
why: Rank estimation tests whether a global algebraic invariant can be recovered from local sparse access.

import_provenance.original_title: Estimating sparse finite-field matrix rank with sublinear queries
import_provenance.original_statement: For n×n matrices over F₂ with O(1) nonzeros in every row and column, how many row/column adjacency queries are needed to estimate rank within additive εn? Yoshida conjectured that Ω(n) queries are necessary in general, despite efficient special cases corresponding to graph incidence matrices.

sentences: A sparse binary matrix is accessed through complete row or column neighborhoods.
The task is to estimate its rank over the two-element field to additive εn error.
The target is adaptive randomized query complexity for fixed sparsity and accuracy.
The source conjectures a linear obstruction in general while recording easier incidence-matrix cases.
Resolving the problem would explain when local sparse observations determine a global algebraic invariant.
